activity.instructions.source: The Hillford council has ideas for using AI. Put each idea in the group you would recommend. There is no score, and more than one answer can make sense. After you place one, you see one possible answer and a reason. Then, as a separate point, you see what the European Union (EU) AI law says.
activity.instructions.back: The Hillford council has some ideas for using AI. Put each idea in the group you recommend. There are no marks, and more than one answer can make sense. After you place one idea, you see one possible answer and one reason. Then, as a separate point, you see what the European Union (EU) AI law says.

read.sections.0.heading.source: Many groups make rules for AI
read.sections.0.heading.back: Many groups make rules for AI

read.sections.0.text.source: New technology brings questions about who it helps, who it might harm and who decides. In the made-up town of Hillford, the council wants to use AI, so it holds a meeting first. A shop owner, students, a nurse, an older neighbour and a newer resident who can't vote all give their views. In the real world, many groups make rules for AI. Governments make laws, which everyone must follow. Companies write rules for their own tools. Groups of countries agree on a guideline, which is advice that countries can choose to use. Residents, including young people, can share their ideas too.
read.sections.0.text.back: New technology brings questions about whom it helps, whom it might harm and who makes the decisions. In Hillford, a made-up town, the town council wants to use AI, so the council holds a meeting first. A shop owner, students, a nurse, an older neighbour and a new resident who cannot vote all give their views. In the real world, many groups make rules for AI. Governments make laws, which everyone must obey. Companies write rules for their own tools. Groups of countries agree on guidelines, which are advice that countries can choose to use. Residents, including young people, can also share their ideas.

read.sections.1.heading.source: Guidelines, a law and levels of risk
read.sections.1.heading.back: Guidelines, laws and levels of risk

read.sections.1.text.source: In 2021, all 193 member states of UNESCO adopted the first global agreement on the ethics of AI, which says AI should protect human rights and stay under human control. In 2024, the countries of ASEAN in Southeast Asia shared a guide for AI, with ideas such as fairness, privacy and safety. Both are guidelines. The European Union (EU) made a law that came into force in August 2024, with parts starting on different dates. It sorts uses of AI by risk, which means how much harm they could do. Some uses are banned, such as scores that treat people unfairly. Some are high risk, such as marking exams, so they need strict checks. Most uses, like spam filters, have no special AI rules, but other laws, like privacy laws, still apply.
read.sections.1.text.back: In 2021, all 193 member states of UNESCO adopted the first global agreement on the ethics of AI, which says AI should protect human rights and stay under human control. In 2024, the ASEAN countries in Southeast Asia shared a guide for AI, with ideas such as fairness, privacy and safety. Both are guidelines. The European Union (EU) made a law that came into force in August 2024, with its parts starting on different dates. That law separates uses of AI by risk, that is, how much harm they can cause. Some uses are banned, such as scores that treat people unfairly. Some are high risk, such as marking exam papers, so strict checks are needed. Most uses, such as spam filters, have no special AI rules, but other laws, such as privacy laws, still apply.

read.sections.2.heading.source: A real service, and your own view
read.sections.2.heading.back: A real service, and your own view

read.sections.2.text.source: In Thailand, people report problems such as broken roads, floods or street lights on Traffy Fondue, a public platform built by a national science agency. Its AI sorts each report and sends it to the right office, where people still decide what to do and fix it. Its makers say it received over 940,000 reports in two years. That shows many people use it, not how well each problem was solved. What a law says is one answer. Your own recommendation can be different, if you give reasons.

watch.summary.source: This video is from UNESCO. UNESCO is a world group that works on schools, science and culture. The video is part of a series about the ethics of AI. Ethics means what is right and wrong. The video asks a big question. How can people get the good things from AI without making gaps between people bigger? AI could also bring new kinds of unfair results. The video says people around the world seem to agree on some ideas. These include privacy, equal treatment and leaving no one out. The hard part is turning these ideas into real rules. The video looks at how different parts of the world are making rules for AI. It also asks what would make rules fair for everyone, everywhere.

educatorNotes.0.source: Keep two questions apart: “What do you recommend for Hillford?” (the learner's view, marked on reasons) and “What does the European Union's law say?” (a fact about one jurisdiction). Never mark a recommendation wrong because it differs from the EU law. The AI Act (in force 1 August 2024) bans, from 2 February 2025, social scoring that leads to unjustified or unrelated harmful treatment, emotion recognition in workplaces and schools except for medical or safety reasons, and live face identification by police in public places except for three narrow purposes (searching for victims or missing persons, preventing an imminent threat, and finding suspects of serious crimes). Transparency rules (chatbots, labelled deepfakes) apply from August 2026. After the AI Omnibus (in force 27 July 2026), high-risk rules for uses such as exam scoring apply from 2 December 2027, and for AI in regulated products from 2 August 2028; check the Commission's page before quoting dates. Minimal-risk uses (spam filters, games) have no AI Act rules, but data protection, consumer protection and product safety law still apply (Article 2). The market-camera item is about police; a council's or shop's face cameras would fall under other rules. Paper version: the nine ideas on cards under three headings.

educatorNotes.1.source: Traffy Fondue (Thailand) was developed by NECTEC, part of the National Science and Technology Development Agency (NSTDA). Residents report through a LINE chatbot with a location and photo; since 2024 its AI also summarises reports, ranks them by urgency, suggests fixes and filters rude words, as well as classifying them and sending each to the responsible agency. NSTDA reports more than 940,000 reports from June 2022 to July 2024, over 733,000 of them “completed” (77%), across 77 provinces and more than 15,000 agencies. These are the operator's own figures: completed is a status in the system, not an independent check of repairs. It is an operating service, not a measured impact.
